name: supastarter
tagline: A paid Next.js SaaS starter kit with auth, teams, billing, emails and i18n already wired together.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as a license for the codebase rather than a subscription.

verdictSummary: This is the one category where the DIY question is almost circular: the product is scaffolding, and scaffolding is exactly what coding agents do best. An agent will happily produce a Next.js app with auth, a Postgres schema, a Stripe checkout flow and a dashboard shell in one session, and it will look convincing. The gap shows up in the parts nobody demos: webhook idempotency, subscription state that survives a failed payment, org invites with correct role checks, transactional email deliverability, and the fact that every one of those integrations breaks on its own schedule. A paid starter is really a subscription to someone else keeping that plumbing current against Next.js, Stripe and auth library churn. Build it yourself if you are shipping one product and enjoy owning the plumbing; buy it if you plan to start five things and never want to re-solve billing.
coreLoopDIY: Scaffold a Next.js app with email plus OAuth login, a Postgres schema for users and organizations, Stripe subscription checkout with a webhook that keeps plan state in sync, and a gated dashboard.
requirements: A Postgres database (local Docker or a hosted free tier)
Stripe test-mode account and API keys for checkout and webhooks
An email sending account (Resend or similar) for magic links and invites
A Google or GitHub OAuth app if you want social login
whatYouLose: Someone else tracking Next.js, Stripe API and auth library breaking changes and shipping the migration for you
Battle-tested billing edge cases: proration, dunning, trials, plan downgrades, tax handling
Docs, a support channel and other people who already hit the bug you are about to hit
The multi-framework and multi-provider variants, so switching your database or auth stack later is on you
Polished extras that always get cut from a one-shot build: admin panel, i18n with RTL, a landing page you do not hate
moatNotes: The moat is maintenance, not code. Any single file in a starter kit is reproducible; the value is that it still compiles after the next major release of everything it touches.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a boilerplate is bought once and reused across projects, so the math is per-idea rather than per-month, and because the second time you wire Stripe webhooks you understand exactly how little you want to do it a third time. Agents generate plausible billing code very fast, and plausible billing code is the worst kind: it works in test mode and quietly desyncs in production. People pay for the assurance that the unglamorous 15 percent was already debugged by someone whose reputation depends on it, plus updates when the underlying frameworks move.
notes: The irony is thick: a paid starter kit competing with the tool whose entire job is starting things. It survives on upkeep, not on the initial scaffold.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted SaaS starter template in an empty folder. This is a codebase I will reuse, so favor clarity over cleverness.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15, App Router, TypeScript, React Server Components where sensible
- Tailwind CSS plus shadcn/ui for components
- Postgres via Drizzle ORM, with a docker-compose.yml for local Postgres
- Auth: better-auth with email magic links plus GitHub OAuth
- Billing: Stripe Checkout plus a webhook handler
- Email: Resend, with a dev fallback that logs the email body to the console

What to build:
1. Schema: users, sessions, organizations, organization_members with roles owner | admin | member, invitations, subscriptions.
2. Auth flows: sign up, sign in, sign out, magic link verification, GitHub OAuth callback. On first sign up, auto-create a personal organization and make the user owner.
3. Org switching: a header dropdown that sets the active org in a cookie. All dashboard queries must be scoped to the active org, enforced server side, never trusted from the client.
4. Invitations: owner or admin can invite an email, which sends a tokenized link that joins the invitee to the org with a chosen role. Tokens expire after 7 days and are single use.
5. Billing: a pricing page with two plans read from Stripe price IDs in env vars. Stripe Checkout for subscribing, Stripe billing portal link for managing. A /api/stripe/webhook route that verifies the signature, handles checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.updated and customer.subscription.deleted, and is idempotent by event id stored in a processed_events table.
6. Gating: a requirePlan helper used by at least one dashboard page, so the pattern is obvious.
7. A minimal marketing landing page and a dashboard shell with settings pages for profile, organization and billing.

Explicitly out of scope: analytics, telemetry, i18n, admin panel, a mobile app, tests beyond a couple of Vitest unit tests on the webhook handler and the role checks.

Rules: all secrets in .env with a committed .env.example, no telemetry, no third-party scripts on the landing page. Include a README with setup steps, migration commands and a Stripe CLI command for testing webhooks locally. Run the migrations and confirm the app boots before you finish.
